samples.text:
Nowadays many tourists travel to famous places mainly because they want to take photos and post them on social media. This essay will explain why this is happening and how it change the experience of travelling.

There are several reasons for this trend. The main reason is the popularity of social media like Instagram and TikTok. People want to show to their friends and followers where they have been, and they feel happy when they get many likes and comments. Secondly, nowadays every person has a smartphone with a good camera, so taking photos is very easy and cheap. In the past, people used film cameras and they could only take few pictures. Also, some places become famous only because they look beautiful in photos, for example colourful streets or special cafés, so tourists go there to take the same picture which they saw online.

This trend changes travelling in several ways, mostly negative. Firstly, tourists spend a lot of time looking at their phone screens instead of enjoy the place. For example, some people visit a beautiful beach but they spend one hour to take selfies and do not relax. Secondly, famous photo spots become very crowded, and tourists have to wait in long queues only for one picture. This can also be a problem for local people who live there. On the other hand, photos can help people to remember their holiday and share their experience with family.

In conclusion, tourists take many photos for social media because it is popular and easy with smartphones. I think this makes travelling less enjoyable because people do not really experience the place, although photos can be a nice memory.
samples.why: Both questions addressed with a clear view · relevant examples but limited depth · basic linking (Secondly, Also) · simple vocabulary (nice, beautiful) · errors with verb forms, prepositions and quantifiers.

samples.text:
In recent years, many travellers seem more concerned with capturing images for social media than with exploring the places they visit. This essay will examine the causes of this development and discuss how it is changing the nature of travel.

The rise of image-based social media platforms is the most obvious cause. Sharing holiday photographs has become a way of presenting an attractive lifestyle to friends and followers, and the positive feedback in the form of likes and comments can be highly rewarding. Travel has therefore become, for some people, a means of building an online identity. At the same time, the tourism industry has adapted to this demand. Hotels, restaurants and even local councils create colourful murals, viewing platforms and other photogenic spots, knowing that shared images act as free advertising. Smartphones with high-quality cameras have also made it effortless to take hundreds of photographs in a single day.

This shift has altered the travel experience in significant ways. For many tourists, the focus has moved from experiencing a place to documenting it, so they may spend more time arranging the perfect shot than appreciating the atmosphere, talking to local people or learning about the history of a site. Travel itineraries are increasingly shaped by what looks impressive on a screen, which means that lesser-known but interesting places can be overlooked. Popular photo spots, meanwhile, become overcrowded, spoiling the visit for other travellers and creating problems for residents. Nevertheless, photography is not entirely negative; it can encourage people to notice details and helps them to preserve memories.

In conclusion, the desire to share images online, the tourism industry's response and easy access to cameras have made photography central to modern tourism. While it helps people record their journeys, it often turns travel into a performance rather than a genuine experience.
samples.why: Clear position with both questions answered and extended · logical progression and effective paragraphing · good range of vocabulary (itineraries, photogenic, overlooked) · frequent error-free sentences with one parallelism slip.

samples.text:
At many famous landmarks, it is now common to see visitors queuing not to enter a building or admire a view, but to reproduce a photograph they have already seen online. This trend reflects the central role of social media in modern life, and it is subtly changing what it means to travel.

The underlying cause is the way image-sharing platforms have turned travel into a form of self-presentation. A holiday was once a private experience, recounted afterwards to a few friends; today it can be broadcast in real time to hundreds of followers, and the approval this generates offers a powerful incentive to seek out striking backdrops. Influencers amplify the effect by popularising particular viewpoints, which then become obligatory stops for their audiences. The tourism industry has been quick to capitalise on this, designing hotels, cafés and attractions with photogenic features precisely because every shared image serves as free promotion. Ubiquitous smartphone cameras, of course, have removed any practical limit on how many pictures can be taken.

The consequences for the experience of travelling are considerable. When the primary goal is to capture an image, attention shifts from the place itself to how it will appear to others, and the unplanned encounters and quiet observation that once defined travel can be crowded out. Itineraries also become more uniform, as visitors converge on the same well-known spots while neighbourhoods without an obvious visual hook are ignored. For residents of popular destinations, this concentration brings congestion, while visitors may arrive only to find a place swamped by others with the same idea. That said, photography can still enrich travel when it encourages people to look closely and preserve meaningful memories rather than simply to accumulate evidence of having been somewhere.

In conclusion, photo-driven tourism has grown out of social media culture, industry marketing and constant access to cameras. While it need not be harmful, it risks turning travel from an act of discovery into a performance staged for an online audience.
samples.why: Both questions answered with insight and a nuanced conclusion · ideas extended and logically sequenced · sophisticated, natural vocabulary (self-presentation, capitalise on, converge) · wide range of structures, error-free.
